options: 'The fact discovered embraces the place from which the object is produced and the knowledge of the accused as to this, and the information given must relate distinctly to this fact'; confession of having killed is strictly excluded
The entire confession including past history of murder is admissible
Section 27 was declared unconstitutional
Section 27 applies only to theft cases
explanation: Pulukuri Kottaya is the locus classicus: fact discovered is physical object + place of concealment + accused's knowledge; the confession of past guilt ('I killed X with this knife') is inadmissible.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; fact discovered = object + place + knowledge; past guilt confession excluded.

provision: BSA S. 23(2) Proviso / IEA S. 27 / Pulukuri Kottaya
learningObjective: Master Pulukuri Kottaya doctrine on Section 27 IEA.

question: An accused in police custody states: 'I have buried the knife with which I stabbed B in the field behind my house, and I will show you where it is'. Which part of this statement is ADMISSIBLE under Section 27 IEA / Section 23(2) Proviso BSA?
options: Only 'I have buried the knife in the field behind my house, and I will show you where it is'; the words 'with which I stabbed B' are strictly inadmissible
The entire sentence is admissible
Nothing is admissible because he was in police custody
Only the word 'knife' is admissible
explanation: Under Pulukuri Kottaya, the confession of past stabbing ('with which I stabbed B') is severed and excluded; only the statement of concealment and location distinctly leading to discovery is admitted.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; words relating to past stabbing are severed and excluded.
optionBreakdown.B: Inculpatory past guilt cannot be smuggled under S. 27.
optionBreakdown.C: Section 27 is an express exception to police custody bar.

learningObjective: Apply Pulukuri Kottaya severability rule to discovery statement.

question: What is the relationship between Section 27 IEA (Section 23(2) Proviso BSA) and Sections 24, 25, 26 IEA?
options: Section 27 is an EXCEPTION or proviso to Sections 24, 25, and 26; it partially lifts the ban on police confessions to the extent that information distinctly leads to discovery of a relevant fact
Section 27 cancels Sections 24, 25 and 26 completely
Sections 25 and 26 override Section 27
Section 27 applies only in civil courts
explanation: State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya (AIR 1960 SC 1125) settled that Section 27 operates as a proviso/exception carving out discovery of facts from the absolute ban of Sections 24-26.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 27 is an exception carving out confirmation by subsequent facts.
optionBreakdown.C: Section 27 prevails to the extent of discovery.

learningObjective: Master Section 27 as exception to Sections 24-26 IEA.

question: In State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya (AIR 1960 SC 1125), the Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of Section 27 IEA under Article 14, holding that:
options: The classification between persons in police custody and persons not in police custody is reasonable and founded on an intelligible differentia with rational relation to the object
Section 27 violates Article 14 and was struck down
Section 27 violates Article 20(3)
Section 27 applies only to Uttar Pradesh
explanation: Deoman Upadhyaya Constitution Bench upheld Section 27 under Article 14: custody status creates a valid classification to ensure discovery reliability.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; upheld under Article 14 on intelligible differentia.

learningObjective: Master Deoman Upadhyaya Article 14 constitutional ruling.

question: In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (AIR 1961 SC 1808), the 11-Judge Constitution Bench held that Section 27 IEA does NOT violate Article 20(3) (right against self-incrimination), because:
options: Giving information leading to discovery of physical facts or giving handwriting/fingerprints does not amount to 'being a witness against oneself' unless compelled
Self-incrimination does not exist in Indian law
Article 20(3) applies only to corporate fraud
Police can use torture to discover weapons
explanation: Kathi Kalu Oghad 11-Judge Bench held that furnishing physical evidence or info leading to discovery is not testimonial compulsion under Art 20(3) unless actual force/torture was used.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; discovery of physical facts does not constitute testimonial compulsion under Art 20(3).

provision: BSA S. 23 / Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) / Art. 20(3)
learningObjective: Master Kathi Kalu Oghad 11-Judge Bench ruling on S. 27 and Article 20(3).

question: Can a discovery under Section 27 IEA be made from an OPEN PUBLIC PLACE accessible to all?
options: No; if the property was discovered from an open public place accessible to anyone (e.g. an open public road or field), it carries no evidentiary weight unless proved hidden or concealed by the accused
Yes, finding anything anywhere is conclusive proof against the accused
Discoveries must only be from inside police stations
Open places are preferred over secret places
explanation: Trimbak v. State of M.P. (AIR 1954 SC 39) established that recovery from an open place accessible to the public does not prove exclusive possession or knowledge of accused.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; recovery from open public place without concealment carries no evidentiary value.

learningObjective: Analyze discovery from open public place under S. 27 IEA.

question: What is the doctrine of 'Confirmation by Subsequent Events' underlying Section 27 IEA?
options: Even though a confession to police is tainted with suspicion, when the information is verified and confirmed by the actual discovery of the physical object at the designated place, the truth of that part is guaranteed
Subsequent events forgive all prior offences
Subsequent discovery permits police to beat the suspect
Any weapon found anywhere confirms the accused's guilt
explanation: The theoretical foundation of Section 27 is the doctrine of confirmation by subsequent facts: physical discovery corroborates the veracity of the information given.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; verification by physical discovery guarantees truth of that part.
optionBreakdown.D: Must be based on accused's distinct information.

learningObjective: Master doctrine of Confirmation by Subsequent Events.

question: If the police ALREADY KNEW where the weapon was hidden before the accused made his statement, can the discovery be proved under Section 27 IEA?
options: No; if the fact was already known to the police, there is NO discovery in consequence of the information given by the accused, and Section 27 cannot apply (Jaffar Hussain Dastagir)
Yes, statement can be recorded post-discovery
Police knowledge is irrelevant
Accused is still presumed to have discovered it
explanation: Jaffar Hussain Dastagir v. State of Maharashtra ((1969) 2 SCC 872) held that discovery must be in consequence of information; if police already knew the place, S. 27 is inapplicable.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; prior police knowledge negates discovery under Section 27.

learningObjective: Master prior police knowledge bar on Section 27 discovery.

question: Must the accused be in 'Custody of a police officer' at the time of giving information under Section 27 IEA / Section 23(2) Proviso BSA?
options: Yes, custody is an express statutory requirement ('received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer')
No, custody is not mentioned in Section 27
Accused must be on bail
Custody must be in the High Court lockup
explanation: Section 27 IEA / Section 23(2) Proviso BSA explicitly requires: 'received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer' (constructive or formal custody).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; police custody is an express statutory requirement.

learningObjective: Recall statutory custody requirement for Section 27 discovery.
